processing: Standard sheng: withered, pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, then pressed or sold loose.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking, as with other Yiwu village tea.
appearance_dry: Long, dark green large leaf with some buds, as usual for Yiwu.
taste_profile: A seller describes it as rich and fresh with a honeyed sweetness; typical of Yiwu, expect a soft broth with little bitterness.

brewing.notes: Yiwu-style tea tolerates slightly longer steeps; a lighter dose shows the honey notes better.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year as single-village sheng, usually spring, and as a component of Yiwu blends. It is usual for Yiwu cakes to be drunk young for their sweetness or kept to age, so a stated year and storage history are what to ask for.
description:
Wangong is a Yiwu village in the Gumanche grouping with Mahei, Luoshuidong, Guafengzhai and Yishangmo. It is named among Yiwu's representative tea places, though much less documented than Mahei or Guafengzhai.

Production follows the ordinary sheng path, and nothing unusual is recorded for this village.

The one specific note available speaks of a rich, fresh cup with honey sweetness. That fits the wider Yiwu description of soft water and low bitterness, but it comes from a seller, so taste for yourself. Slightly longer steeps than for a Bulang tea work well.

Look for a stated year and village, and compare it with a Mahei to see whether the differences within Yiwu matter to you.
history: Wangong appears in lists of Yiwu tea villages and old tea sites, within the mountain that served as a main collecting point for the Qing-era trade. Little is documented about the village's own tea history.
